stance_basis: letter supports EO 11644's spirit but demands stronger regulations and improved EIS addressing Alaska-specific concerns
summary: The Alaska Conservation Society submitted a formal comment letter supporting the philosophy behind Executive Order 11644 but expressing significant concerns about the quality of the Draft Environmental Impact Statement and the adequacy of proposed regulations. They raised specific issues about the EIS being poorly written, the need to regulate non-recreational ORV uses, ambiguity in BLM land classification, and the absence of any discussion of Alaska's unique permafrost and tundra ecosystems. They called for stronger, more comprehensive regulations to protect Alaska's public lands.
complaint_summary: The Alaska Conservation Society supports EO 11644 in principle but criticizes the Draft EIS as poorly written and fragmentary, argues regulations must cover non-recreational ORV uses (mineral/petroleum exploration, government surveys), faults the ambiguous open/closed classification for BLM lands, and objects to the complete omission of Alaska's unique permafrost and tundra ecosystems from the impact analysis.

statement.text:
The Alaska Conservation Society appreciates the spirit and philosophy behind E. O. 11644 establishing the basis for departmental control of off-road vehicle use on all of our public lands. Because of the vast proportion of Alaska's lands within the public domain, and because of the present and potential damage to the tundra and boreal forest ecosystems, and their wildlife resources, we are anxious to see that strong regulations are promulgated.
The Draft Environmental Impact Statement prepared by your Bureau applies to all Interior Agencies, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation, Bureau of Land Management, Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife, National Park Service and the Bureau of Reclamation. Because of the importance of these agencies in the management of Alaska's public lands, we offer the following comments for your review and consideration.

Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation July 6, 1972 Page Two
1. The draft environmental impact statement appears to be generally poorly written and fragmentary. The mention of various "impacts", both environmental and economic, and both positive and negative, is poorly developed and little or no attempt is made to relate these impacts to one another quantitatively. The discussion of the economic impacts of ORV is useless, as well as fragmentary throughout the entire document. The concept that ORV use could aid in strengthening family relationships, mentioned several times in the statement, is undocumented and, in truth, use of ORV by young people may contribute to the destruction of the American family that has paralleled the evolution of the automobile.
2. The Preamble to E.O. 11644 refers specifically to "recreational" vehicles. The subsequent statements refer to off-road vehicles without the qualifier "recreational". The regualtions should apply to all vehicles, including official use by governmental agencies, etc. Throughout Alaska, much of the damage done by ORV is the direct result of mineral and petroleum exploration, government-sponsored surveys, forestry activities and construction equipment. It is essential that these uses be adequately regulated, in addition to recreational uses. We recognize that the use of ORV for emergency fire or law enforcement and other such purposes may be needed, however, the increasing use of aircraft in these cases may soon preclude much of the ORV use.
3. Since the issuance of E.O. 11644, considerable confusion has arisen concerning whether lands will be classified as "open unless otherwise designated" or "closed unless otherwise designated". The statement partially clarifies this problem by stating that Wilderness and Primitive Areas are closed, and that trails and areas will be established in National Parks, Monuments, Natural Areas, and National Wildlife Refuges and Ranges only if the Bureau head so decides.
However, the Bureau of Land Management and Bureau of Reclamation lands appear open to access unless closed (except for Bureau of Land Management Primitive Areas). The

Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation July 6, 1972 Page Three
The statement is made in Memorandum K-14 that "Areas and trails shall not be located in areas possessing unique natural, wildlife, historic or recreational values unless the Bureau head determines that these unique values will not be adversely affected". This statement is not referred to in the outlining of the Bureau of Land Management's responsibilities in DES 72-62, thus leaving the criteria for Bureau of Land Management classification vague.
4. Although various criteria are mentioned by which Bureaus will establish open and closed areas, no mention is made of the unique Alaskan tundra and Boreal forest permafrost regime. In summer, ORV travel on permafrost-underlain areas can be severely destructive, as permafrost, once thawed, may never reform. Travel over a deep winter snowbed is less destructive, although compression of the snow layer and thin vegetative mat may result in damage to the plant covering. Although research into this possible damage is still continuing, it may be possible to open some areas in winter, and close them the remainder of the year. This technique has proven somewhat effective on the North Slope of Alaska.
I realize that the above comments are, by no means, a comprehensive criticism of DES 72-62. However, I hope our suggestions will result in an improved, stronger statement and policy for use of ORV on our public lands.
Sincerely,
ALASKA CONSERVATION SOCIETY
Ernst Mueller President
